q: You apply a valid Ingress to a fresh kind cluster and nothing happens: no address, no routing, no errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: No Ingress controller is installed (or none serves the `ingressClassName`)
The Ingress API is deprecated and disabled by default
kind does not support Layer 7 traffic
The Service must be of type `LoadBalancer` for an Ingress to work
explain: Kubernetes ships the Ingress *API* but no implementation. Without a controller watching that IngressClass, the object just sits in etcd. Backends are normally ClusterIP Services.

q: Which statements about the 2026 ingress-nginx retirement are accurate? (select all)
options: The community `kubernetes/ingress-nginx` controller stopped receiving releases and security fixes after March 2026
The Ingress API (`networking.k8s.io/v1`) was removed from Kubernetes
Existing installations keep working, but will not get CVE fixes
F5's NGINX Ingress Controller is a separate product and was not part of this retirement
Gateway API is the recommended migration target
explain: Only the community controller was retired (best-effort maintenance until March 2026, then repos read-only). The Ingress API remains GA. F5's controller is a different project. Kubernetes recommends Gateway API, with `ingress2gateway` to help convert.

q: In Gateway API's role-oriented model, which resource is typically owned by application developers?
explain: Infra providers own GatewayClass, cluster operators own Gateways (listeners, TLS, which namespaces may attach), and app teams own HTTPRoutes in their namespaces.

q: An HTTPRoute in namespace `shop` points at Gateway `infra/edge`. Its status shows `Accepted=False` with reason `NotAllowedByListeners`. The Gateway listener has no `allowedRoutes` field. What is the fix?
options: Set `allowedRoutes.namespaces.from` to `All` or a `Selector` matching `shop` on the listener
explain: `allowedRoutes` defaults to `from: Same`, so only routes in `infra` can attach. Route attachment is controlled by the Gateway's `allowedRoutes`, not by ReferenceGrant. ReferenceGrant is for references to objects such as Services or Secrets in another namespace.

q: A route in `shop` has a `backendRef` to Service `payments-api` in namespace `payments`. Status: `ResolvedRefs=False`, reason `RefNotPermitted`. Where must the ReferenceGrant be created?
options: In `payments`, with `from` = HTTPRoute in `shop` and `to` = Service
explain: The referenced side consents: the ReferenceGrant lives in the target namespace (`payments`) and lists who may reference what. This stops one team from pointing traffic at another team's Services without permission.

q: You want 10% of `/api` traffic to go to `api-v2`. Which HTTPRoute feature do you use?
options: Two rules with identical matches; the proxy alternates
`weight` on each `backendRef` in the same rule (for example 90 and 10)
explain: Weighted `backendRefs` split traffic proportionally (weights are relative). `RequestMirror` copies traffic to a shadow backend but its responses are discarded, so users never see v2.

q: Which of these are core HTTPRoute filters defined by the Gateway API spec (not implementation-specific)? (select all)
explain: Redirects, rewrites, header modifiers and mirroring are in the spec. Rate limiting is implementation-specific (for example Envoy Gateway's `BackendTrafficPolicy`).

q: A listener has `hostname: "*.example.com"`. Which route hostnames can attach to it? (select all)
explain: In Gateway API a leading `*.` is a **suffix match**: `*.example.com` matches `api.example.com` and `a.b.example.com`, but not the apex `example.com`. Note the difference from TLS certificates, where a wildcard SAN covers exactly one label, so a `*.example.com` certificate would not be valid for `a.b.example.com`.

q: Why does the local TLS setup create a CA certificate with cert-manager instead of issuing self-signed leaf certificates directly?
options: You trust one CA certificate once, and every leaf it signs is trusted, the same way production works with a public CA
explain: Each self-signed leaf would have to be trusted individually. With a CA issuer, you pass `--cacert` (or add the CA to Keychain) once and all leaf certs validate.

q: An HTTPRoute's backendRef uses `port: 5678`, the container port, while the Service exposes `port: 80, targetPort: 5678`. What happens?
options: It works; Gateway API uses container ports
Kubernetes rejects the HTTPRoute at admission
The controller rewrites it to 80 automatically
The backend is not resolved correctly and requests fail, because `backendRefs.port` is the Service port
explain: Like Ingress, `backendRefs.port` refers to the Service port. A port the Service does not expose cannot be resolved; you typically see a status condition and 500/503 responses.

q: You are on kind with Envoy Gateway. The Gateway's Envoy Service shows `EXTERNAL-IP <pending>`. How can you reach it from your Mac? (select all)
options: Run cloud-provider-kind on the host to assign LoadBalancer addresses
It is unreachable until you deploy to a cloud provider
explain: kind has no cloud LB, so the Service stays pending, but port-forwarding, cloud-provider-kind, or a NodePort mapped through `extraPortMappings` all work.

q: Your NestJS API behind the Gateway logs every request as coming from the same IP, which breaks per-client rate limiting. What should you check?
options: Whether the HTTPRoute uses `PathPrefix` instead of `Exact`
That the proxy sets `X-Forwarded-For` correctly and the app is configured to trust the proxy (`trust proxy`)
That the pods have a readiness probe
explain: The app sees the proxy's connection. The real client IP arrives in `X-Forwarded-For` (or PROXY protocol from the LB). Express/NestJS only use it when `trust proxy` is configured, so the proxy hops must be trusted explicitly.

q: Which status condition tells you a Gateway's data plane has been configured by its controller?
explain: `Programmed=True` on a Gateway means the controller has configured the underlying proxy. `ResolvedRefs` applies to routes and listeners (references resolved); `Accepted` means the config is valid.
